title: Open Problem (interference worsens with depth)
statement_text: We believe that it is also the case that interference gets worst with $r$ (namely that interference worsens as $r$ increases to $r+1$ for $r > 2$), although whether this is indeed the case is an open problem.
context_text: A network of depth 2 is a bipartite graph $G=(A\cup B,E)$ with $|A|=|B|=n$ (inputs and outputs, edges being tasks); a task set to be performed in parallel is a matching, and it can be performed without interference if it is an induced matching (no edge of $G$ joins two of its edges). $G$ is a $(k,\alpha(k))$-multitasker if every matching $M$ of size $k$ contains an induced matching $M'\subseteq M$ with $|M'|\ge\alpha(k)|M|$, and an $\alpha$-multitasker if this holds with $\alpha$ for all $k=1,\dots,n$; $\alpha(k)\in(0,1]$ is the multitasking capacity. A network with $r$ layers (depth $r$) of width $n$ and degree $d$ has vertex set partitioned into independent sets $V_1,\dots,V_r$ of size $n$, consecutive layers inducing $d$-regular bipartite graphs and no other edges; task sets are families of vertex-disjoint top-bottom paths $v_1\dots v_r$ ($v_i\in V_i$), and such a family is induced if no edge of $G$ joins edges of two different paths; the multitasking capacity is defined as before with induced path families in place of induced matchings. For $d$-regular bipartite (depth 2) graphs the authors prove $\alpha(n)=O(1/\sqrt d)$; for depth $r$ they prove that the capacity for task sets of size $n$ is $O(r/d^{1-1/r})$, so depth-$r$ networks with $2<r\ll d$ suffer strictly more interference than depth-2 networks ($r$ is thought of as a constant and $d\to\infty$). The open problem is whether the capacity keeps getting worse at each step from $r$ to $r+1$ for $r>2$.

title: Open Problem (multitasker at average degree $\Theta(\log n)$)
statement_text: It is an interesting question whether there exists a multitasker with $\alpha > 0$ independent of $n$, for average degree $\Theta(\log n)$, which, if true is the largest average degree possible. This is left as an open problem.
context_text: A network of depth 2 is a bipartite graph $G=(A\cup B,E)$ with $|A|=|B|=n$ (inputs and outputs, edges being tasks); a task set to be performed in parallel is a matching, and it can be performed without interference if it is an induced matching (no edge of $G$ joins two of its edges). $G$ is a $(k,\alpha(k))$-multitasker if every matching $M$ of size $k$ contains an induced matching $M'\subseteq M$ with $|M'|\ge\alpha(k)|M|$, and an $\alpha$-multitasker if this holds with $\alpha$ for all $k=1,\dots,n$; $\alpha(k)\in(0,1]$ is the multitasking capacity. Here $n$ is the number of vertices on each side, $\alpha>0$ independent of $n$ means a fixed constant capacity, and the graphs need not be regular. The authors prove that every $\alpha$-multitasker of average degree $d$ satisfies $\alpha\le O((\log n/d)^{1/3})$, so average degree $\Theta(\log n)$ is the largest possible for constant $\alpha$; for $d$-regular graphs the capacity even satisfies $\alpha(n)=O(1/\sqrt d)$. On the other hand there are multitaskers of average degree $\Omega(\log\log n)$ with $\alpha>1/3-\varepsilon$, so for the capacity to decay with the average degree one must assume $d$ grows faster than $\log\log n$. The question is whether constant-capacity multitaskers exist with average degree $\Theta(\log n)$.
